Dead Cells is probably my favorite *whatever*. Metroidvania? Rougelite? Platformer? Its all three in equal measure, and it does a fantastic job of blending them together in a rewarding way that seems to keep the player coming back for more punishment. The gameplay will largely revolve around what build you want to play, and features a really fun system with three archtypes that you can either focus individually on, or blend at your discretion. This system rewards experimentation, and you'll be unlocking new items and abilities as you progress. Weapons, magical abilities, passive/active buffs, traps, companions, and the means of unlocking new routes thru the game. I really enjoy the way this game *works*. 

There's always a part in my reviews where I say something akin to "this game is eye candy", and I feel the same way about Dead Cells. Most of this game is visually stunning, provided you enjoy pixel graphics. Light is thoughtfully distributed throughout the dark tunnels, stretching corridors and dead keeps of the castle walls. Each of the "biomes" are visually unique, sporting bright and well placed colors that please the ape brain. This only reinforces the varying challenges that different routes can present the player. I'm a sucker for good parallax scrolling and this game masterfully uses multiple layers in some areas to make the land feel expansive and lived in.

The story is probably the weakest part of Dead Cells, but I don't consider that to be a hard negative. While most of the "big reveal" is pretty upfront, there's a ton of hidden backstory and implications that revolve around the player character, the kingdom, and the king who ran it. I thought that was pretty fun, as I tend to enjoy *earning* my story breadcrumbs at a time. What I DON'T like about this is it means most people will never see the full picture, because they won't feel like completing this very challenging game upwards of 5 times, scrounging for flavor text and bits of lore along the way.

All in all this is a fantastic (now unhidden) gem that finds itself in my rotation every few years. 8/10

Important for it's time, but also kind of overrated. A very "meh" thumbs-up.

The part that Dead Cells does well is that it actually tries to incorporate slightly different playstyle mechanics into it's myriad unlockable weapons and items. And this is neat because it shows the developers actually taking a moment to think about how weapons and mechanics from other platformers might mesh with their own game. This makes the game feel much less like a clumsy 'kitchen sink' crossover and instead actually influences how you might change your playstyle per-run or run-to-run.

The part that Dead Cells does badly is that the platforming gamefeel of it's native game just isn't that great. It's floaty and slippery. Damage scaling is utterly absurd in the sense that on later difficulty levels it is very very easy to go from full health to instantly-dead within just a second or two of being caught in between enemy attacks due to the nearly nonexistant contact iframes that one normally sees in a platformer of this kind.

There's perhaps an argument that this is where the more 'rogue' elements of the genre are paramount, that it's intended to foster a more careful play style and the development of a higher skill level. But for what, exactly? Replaying the same biomes again and again on an even higher difficulty level with even more masochistic gameplay? There isn't really a 'living' story of any note. Background details and 'lore' areas occasionally suggest at one which the game is otherwise fundamentally uninterested in exploring further. The entire last DLC literally just gave up and said 'We're doing Castlevania now'.

As one of the first notable examples of the genre, I applaud it's innovation. And the inclusion of so many different accessibility and custom run options is absolutely solid on the part of the developer. And so while I appreciate coming back and revisiting it ten years later, it's just not a game that's near and dear to my heart despite the clear passion that went into making it.

I know Dead Cells is incredibly popular, but I honestly don't understand the overwhelming praise. The combat is fast and responsive, and the pixel art looks great, but once the initial excitement wears off, the game becomes an exhausting cycle of doing the same thing over and over again.

The biggest issue for me is how repetitive everything feels. Dying and starting over is obviously part of the roguelite formula, but that doesn't automatically make it enjoyable. Losing a good run and having to fight through familiar areas and enemies again becomes more frustrating than rewarding. The game expects you to enjoy repetition simply because each run is slightly different, but those differences weren't enough to keep me interested.

The difficulty also feels unnecessarily punishing at times. There's a difference between a challenging game that encourages you to improve and one that makes progress feel like a chore. Unlocking new weapons and abilities should make things more exciting, but the constant grind takes away much of that satisfaction.

I can appreciate the amount of work that went into the game, and I understand why some people love it. Unfortunately, I found the overall experience more tedious than fun.

Short version: I'm no expert in the genre, but I'd probably put this on the Rushmore of runs-based roguelites with Hades, Rogue Legacy and Spelunky.

Longer: I went into this game thinking - perhaps due to the description on the storepage or the use-defined tag that stated as such - that this was a Metroidvania. It's not, not at all. There's very, very little backtracking and, similarly, no movement-unlocks that further open the world up to you. It is no more a Metroidvania than Rogue Legacy 2 would be (which, I see now, *also* has that user-defined tag; perhaps gamers just see a simple map and think 'ah, yep, that's the Metroid there').

What Dead Cells actually does, it does very well: it's a fun runs-based roguelite experience. It's frenetic, chaotic and a very good time. I have my issues with it (mostly movement related: you get 'locked out' of a double jump after falling long enough, your character feels a bit floating, you magnetically gravitate towards ladders if you hit down on a pass-through platform), but for anyone who likes runs-based games, this will certainly scratch the itch.

That said, I *don't* love runs-based roguelites, haha. I think that I'm probably done after completing it once. I am certain there's much, much more that is on offer here.
